reported.text: Easy OA problem (titled like Buy and Sell Stock II but unrelated): pick the highest-value packets alternately from odd and even indices within a fixed budget.
Given a string of length up to 1e5, count the ways to partition it so that every part contains the same number of distinct characters.
Arcs around a wheel should total 360 degrees; replace exactly one arc[i] with shim[i] and pay rate times the shortfall or excess. Minimize the cost (prefix/net sum).
Units must pass station 1 (a[i]) then station 2 (b[i]); choose the order (and erase exactly one b[i]) to minimize total time. The statement referenced Johnson's rule.
On a sorted array, jumping from i to j costs (a[i]-a[j])^2 + b[j]; reach index n-1 with at most K jumps at minimum cost. Needs convex hull trick DP optimization.
Given an array of 0s, 1s and 2s, arrange it so all 1s and all 2s are grouped, where swapping a 1 with a 2 costs 1 and swaps involving 0 are free; find the minimum cost.

Infosys 2026 OA — Were the 4 Coding Questions Actually in Increasing Difficulty?
I recently appeared for the Infosys 2026 coding assessment. There were 4 coding questions, and I found the difficulty quite interesting.

I don't remember seeing any difficulty labels such as Easy/Medium/Hard/Complex on the platform, so I'm curious whether the questions were intentionally arranged in increasing order of difficulty or if the ordering was arbitrary.

Here is what I encountered:

Q1 — DP + Segment Tree

This involved a DP solution where a Segment Tree was needed to efficiently handle the transitions/range queries.

I would personally consider this Hard/Complex because it involves DP + Segment Tree + Binary Search combination.

Q2 — Array containing 0, 1 and 2

The problem involved arranging the elements so that all 1s and all 2s are grouped, where swapping a 1 with a 2 costs 1, while swapping with 0 does not count.

This felt comparatively easier and was mainly based on finding the right observation and calculating the minimum swaps.

I would personally rate this around Easy/Medium.

Q3 — DP with State Optimization

This was another DP problem where a straightforward state/transition approach was not sufficient for the larger constraints, and the DP needed to be optimized.

I would rate this as Hard.

Q4 — Number Transformation / State Space

Given num <= 10^9 and s <= 60, there were two operations:

If num is even, replace it with num / 2
If num > 0, replace it with num - 1

The task was to perform the operations and count the distinct numbers encountered.

Initially, I thought the state space might become very large, but a BFS with a HashSet/visited set works because the number of reachable states is surprisingly small.

I would rate this around Medium.

My personal difficulty ranking

If I had to classify them independently:

Q2 → Easy/Medium
Q4 → Medium
Q3 → Hard
Q1 → Complex

So the questions do not appear to be in increasing order of difficulty based on my experience.

I'm curious about other candidates' experiences:

Were your 4 questions also ordered similarly, or did you get a different ordering/set of problems?

Also, if anyone has a better difficulty rating for these questions, I'd be interested to hear your opinion.

reported.text: Starting from num (up to 1e9) with s up to 60 operations, you may halve num if even or subtract 1 if positive; count the distinct numbers that can be reached (BFS with a visited set works).
